# Evidence: the French-speaking market

Ratings: **Measured** (study or large dataset with method), **Survey** (self-report with a stated sample),
**Practice** (practitioners or official style bodies, no measurement), **Vendor** (a seller's own data or claims),
**Untraced** (no primary source found, or the source does not say it). Regulator statements are marked
**Official**: they say what the rule is, not how a court will apply it. URLs are in `sources.md`.

## Address form (vous or tu)

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| No published A/B test compares tu and vous on B2B reply or acceptance rates | Searches across vendors (Waalaxy, lemlist, La Growth Machine, Overloop) and academic sources, 2026-10-29 | Absence checked (not proof none exists) |
| Informal address is preferred and works better for warm brands, formal for competent brands; six experiments, several languages, consumer settings | Lenoir, ERIM thesis, 2015 | Measured (consumer, not B2B) |
| In French workplaces vous is the default with strangers and in hierarchy; the switch is the hard part | Clyne, Norrby and Warren 2009 (see ../voice) | Measured (interviews and focus groups) |
| 56% of French employees use tu with their direct boss, 64% of managers | Bruneau / TNS Sofres 2013, 604 employees, via search summary only; not in the Welcome to the Jungle article | Untraced |
| About 63% in the private sector use tu with their N+1 against 43% in the public sector; 70% of men against 49% of women | Alex Alber, via Welcome to the Jungle article (read) | Survey (primary not read) |
| In Quebec, vous is usual at a first meeting; keeping vous until the switch is raised is the cautious choice; the older or higher-ranked person proposes tu | OQLF | Practice (official language body) |
| Tu at a first meeting is far more common in Quebec than in other French-speaking regions | OQLF, via search summary of the same page | Practice |
| Swiss Romandie: both forms coexist; the unwritten rule is to wait for the manager to propose tu; tech and start-ups use tu quasi-universally; private banks, law firms keep vous at least with senior management | Upreer guide, June 2026 | Practice (weak, anonymous guide) |
| "Vous + prénom" is very common in Romandie | Ibani guide, via search summary | Practice (weak) |
| Belgium is more informal than France in business | One French-as-foreign-language textbook; contradicted by other sources | Untraced |
| Use tu only if the target and sector fit (creative, young, start-up), otherwise vous | Waalaxy; Overloop; Zeliq | Vendor practice |
| Use formal French, "vous", "Madame, Monsieur" if the name is unknown | Origami, 2026 | Vendor practice |

## Law

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| B2B electronic prospecting needs no prior consent if related to the person's job, the person is told the data's origin and the message's purpose, and can refuse simply | CNIL page dated 10 June 2026 | Official |
| Channels named: email, SMS, MMS, automated calls "and other technologies"; social messaging not named | Same | Official |
| Every commercial message must state on whose behalf it is sent | CNIL 2009; CPCE L34-5 via legal summaries | Official |
| The legal definition of courrier électronique covers any text, voice, sound or image message stored until fetched | LCEN 2004, via LAGBD | Official (read in summary) |
| A LinkedIn private message falls under L34-5 | No text or decision found either way | Untraced |
| B2B electronic prospecting of people contacted for their specific professional activity can rest on legitimate interest, within reasonable expectations | CNIL 2024 recommendations, sheet 2 | Official |
| Source site terms that forbid collection for prospecting put it outside reasonable expectations | Same | Official |
| Content on a professional social network is a priori not essentially personal content | Same | Official |
| Information must be given individually, at the latest at first contact and within one month, naming the source sites where known | Same | Official |
| Do not contact people who objected or are on opposition lists | Same; CNIL 2020 | Official |
| General acceptance of a site's terms is not specific consent | CNIL 2020 and 2024 | Official |
| Collecting LinkedIn contact details that members restricted exceeds reasonable expectations; KASPR fined EUR 240,000 (SAN-2024-020, 5 Dec 2024); about 160 million contacts | CNIL | Official |
| Nestor fined EUR 20,000 for prospecting emails without consent (SAN-2020-018, 8 Dec 2020) | Maddyness, enforcement tracker | Official (read in summary) |
| Belgium: no opt-in for emails to legal entities only where contact details are not linked to an individual | Younity on Lexgo, 2017 | Practice (law firm reading) |
| Belgian e-advertising rules now sit in the Code of Economic Law VI.110 and following | Belgian DPA, via search summary | Official (summary) |
| Switzerland: mass advertising by telecom needs prior consent, a correct sender and an easy free refusal (UCA 3(1)(o), since 1 April 2007) | BAKOM | Official |
| The Swiss rule applies to B2B and B2C alike | Certified Senders Alliance; webinar slides | Practice (secondary) |
| A single individually written message is not "mass advertising" in Switzerland | No source found | Untraced |
| Canada: LinkedIn messaging counts as sending to an electronic address under CASL | CRTC FAQ, via search summary (page 403) | Official (read in summary) |
| Canada: implied consent from conspicuous publication requires that the address carries no "no solicitation" statement and that the message is relevant to the role; publication by a third party alone does not create it; the sender must prove the elements (balance of probabilities) | CRTC infographics, Bennett Jones (read), Gowling | Official / Practice |
| France: consent for consumer cold calls from August 2026; professionals keep a right to object | Secondary commentary | Untraced (official text not read) |
